reference.source: ICHD-3 / Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A group of primary headaches characterised by strictly unilateral pain in the trigeminal distribution, usually the ophthalmic division, with prominent ipsilateral cranial autonomic features
The group comprises cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks (SUNCT and SUNA) and hemicrania continua

Ipsilateral autonomic signs include conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, forehead and facial sweating, miosis and ptosis, while restlessness and agitation are typical of cluster headache

The subtypes are distinguished mainly by attack duration and frequency: cluster is the longest with circadian and circannual clustering, paroxysmal hemicrania has many shorter attacks per day, SUNCT and SUNA are very brief but very frequent, and hemicrania continua is continuous with exacerbations

Treatment response is a defining clue, as paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua show an absolute response to indometacin, while cluster headache responds to high-flow oxygen and triptans with preventives such as verapamil
SUNCT and SUNA can be triggered by cutaneous stimuli and may mimic trigeminal neuralgia, but the conjunctival injection and tearing help differentiate them

A symptomatic (secondary) trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, especially from a pituitary or posterior fossa lesion, must be excluded, so MRI including dedicated pituitary views is recommended, particularly with atypical features
Accurate classification is essential because management differs markedly between the subtypes
reference.pathophysiology: The trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias arise from activation of the trigeminovascular system, referring pain to the ophthalmic trigeminal territory, together with activation of the trigeminal-autonomic (parasympathetic) reflex that produces the ipsilateral cranial autonomic features. Functional imaging implicates the posterior hypothalamus as a generator or permissive region, which underlies the striking circadian and circannual rhythmicity of cluster headache. Parasympathetic outflow via the sphenopalatine ganglion mediates the lacrimation and nasal symptoms, while associated sympathetic dysfunction produces the partial Horner features of ptosis and miosis.
additionalDifferentials: Trigeminal neuralgia, especially in relation to SUNCT and SUNA
Migraine, which may have some autonomic features but a different phenotype
Symptomatic trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia from a pituitary tumour, cavernous sinus or posterior fossa lesion or carotid dissection
Acute angle-closure glaucoma or other ocular and orbital pathology
Sinusitis or dental pathology as non-neurological causes of facial pain
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain with dedicated pituitary and cavernous sinus views to exclude a symptomatic cause
MR or CT angiography if arterial dissection or a vascular lesion is suspected
Detailed headache diary documenting attack duration, frequency, timing and autonomic features
A trial of indometacin where paroxysmal hemicrania or hemicrania continua is suspected
Pituitary function tests if a sellar lesion is found or suspected
Ophthalmological or ENT assessment to exclude a local cause of a red, watering eye
redFlags: A new or atypical presentation, or a change in an established pattern, suggesting a secondary cause
Persistent focal neurological deficit, visual field loss or a fixed Horner syndrome
Features of raised intracranial pressure or a posterior fossa or sellar mass
An unusual age of onset or accompanying systemic symptoms
A painful red eye requiring exclusion of acute glaucoma
reference.prognosis: The trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias are typically chronic or relapsing conditions; with correct classification most respond well to targeted therapy, although some patients develop chronic or refractory disease requiring specialist or neuromodulation approaches.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing cluster headache as migraine or sinusitis and delaying effective treatment
Not performing an indometacin trial and missing an eminently treatable paroxysmal hemicrania or hemicrania continua
Failing to image, including the pituitary, and overlooking a symptomatic trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia
Confusing SUNCT or SUNA with trigeminal neuralgia and managing it incorrectly
Overusing acute medications and precipitating medication-overuse headache
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Abort cluster headache attacks with high-flow oxygen and a fast-acting subcutaneous or intranasal triptan such as sumatriptan or zolmitriptan

Prevent cluster headache with verapamil under ECG monitoring, using a short corticosteroid course or greater occipital nerve block as a transitional bridge, and lithium, topiramate or a CGRP monoclonal antibody as alternatives
Treat suspected paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua with indometacin under gastroprotection, exploiting the absolute response that is both therapeutic and diagnostic
Manage SUNCT and SUNA with lamotrigine or other antiseizure agents, reserving intravenous lidocaine for severe exacerbations
Exclude a symptomatic secondary cause with brain MRI including dedicated pituitary and cavernous-sinus views before committing to long-term treatment
Offer neuromodulation such as occipital nerve or sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation or non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation for refractory disease
Advise avoidance of alcohol and other triggers during cluster bouts, keep a headache diary and refer to a neurology or headache specialist
